params.text:
Introduction

Respect for privacy and confidentiality is a professional responsibility of medical practitioners, since ancient times, but also a standard responsibility of researchers. And that because it is necessary for the protection of personal autonomy and to allow subjects to have control over their personal information. The GDPR and the implementing bylaws in EU Member States provide rules for scientific research. Also, laws on medical secrecy which are applicable to medical doctors complement the data protection legislation as far as medical research is concerned. A specific challenge to confidentiality is raised by cloud computing used for research purposes. In that case, where sensitive data are transferred to a cloud service provider for scientific research, it is crucial to consider stringent data protection measures.

Target audience

These groups will benefit from tailored, accessible content that enhances their knowledge, compliance practices, and decision-making abilities in research ethics, contributing to a more inclusive and responsible research community.

params.text: In today’s diverse and complex research landscape, the use of sensitive personal data for scientific research must be subject to protection measures, in order to safeguard security and confidentiality. The purpose of this learning module is to educate researchers, ethics professionals, and students on the importance of data protection rules and of medical secrecy. It aims to ensure understanding of how to implement the GDPR rules and the rules on medical secrecy and in addition, how to provide protection when using cloud computing for the purposes of a research project.

The purpose of this module is to equip participants with practical knowledge and tools to ensure safety and confidentiality.

By the end of this module, participants will be able to:

  • Understand core principles of privacy and confidentiality, in particular in the framework of the GDPR.
  • Define medical secrecy and its legal and ethical implications in the context of patient privacy and scientific research.
  • Recognize and describe the provisions of the GDPR related to privacy and confidentiality in the context of scientific research.
  • Outline the roles and responsibilities of researchers, data controllers, and data processors under GDPR.
  • Recognize the potential risks to privacy and confidentiality, including data breaches and unauthorized access.
  • Recommend best practices for ensuring compliance with GDPR while preserving the integrity and confidentiality of research data.

params.text:
Privacy and Confidentiality

Privacy in Research

Privacy has been defined as ‘the right to be let alone’, i.e. the right to be free from intrusion by third persons, but in the modern context it is considered as the right to protect any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural (living) person, including electronic communications data.

Confidentiality

Confidentiality is closely related to privacy, and it is also included in the principles of the GDPR (Article 5 para. 1 lit. f). In research activities, subjects communicate sensitive personal data to researchers, which are used for research purposes. Referring to data subject’ personal information as confidential signifies that those who receive it are obligated to safeguard it from being disclosed to individuals who are not authorized to access it.

Researchers can breach confidentiality intentionally by directly disclosing personal information of to an unauthorized person or inadvertently by discussing research participants’ information in that way that an unauthorized person gains knowledge.

params.text:
Most Important Data Protection Principles in Research

The most important principles established in the GDPR which are related to scientific research are the following:
Lawfulness of the Processing Activities: researchers must have a valid lawful basis to process personal data for research purposes.

Rights of Data Subjects: the GDPR strives for transparency and to give control to data subjects over their personal data; for this purpose, it establishes data subjects’ rights such as the right of access, etc.

Records of Processing Activities: Researchers acting as Controllers must implement records of their processing activities which would be used to prove compliance with the GDPR towards the Supervisory Authorities

Data Protection Impact Assessment: where data processing is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of the data subjects, entities must carry out a preventive Data Protection Impact Assessment to identify appropriate measures for mitigating the risks to data protection.

Designation of Data Protection Officer (DPO): if the core activities an entity consist of regular and systematic monitoring of data subjects or of processing special categories of personal data such as health data on a large scale, then a DPO must be designated.
Technical and organizational measures: researchers must implement technical and organisational measures to guarantee the integrity and confidentiality of personal data.

Legal Bases for Processing of Personal Data

In accordance with Article 5 (1) lit. a GDPR, personal data shall be processed lawfully, fairly and in a transparent manner in relation to the data subject. To process personal data lawfully, data controllers need to find the most appropriate legal basis for processing.

Article 6 (1) provides for six lawful grounds for processing. EU Member States cannot add more legal bases to this list, according to CJEU case C‑582/14 (Breyer v. Bundesrepublik Deutschland). Namely, processing personal data is permitted if at least one of the following applies:

params.textField:
*Consent* : The data subject has given clear, informed, and specific consent.

*Contract* : Necessary for a contract with the data subject or pre-contractual steps. 

*Legal Obligation*  : Required to comply with a legal obligation.

*Vital Interests* : Protects someone’s life or safety. 

*Public Interest/Authority* : Needed for tasks in the public interest or official authority. 

*Legitimate Interests* : Benefits the controller or third party without overriding the data subject’s rights, especially for children.

params.text:
Legal Grounds for the Processing of Personal Data for Scientific Purposes

  • The legal grounds that can be used to process personal data for scientific purposes are the following: The consent of the research participant for the purposes of a particular research; consent must be specific to the purpose which must be explained to data subjects.
  • The legitimate interests of the data controller (or a third party). This holds true where the research aims to provide meaningful benefits, such as advancements in medicine, public health, or social understanding, which justify the processing under legitimate interest.; and
  • The performance of a public interest task or exercise of official authority. This the case where the processing is authorized by law or a regulation that explicitly identifies scientific research as a task in the public interest or under official authority.

Legitimate interest

Under the GDPR, researchers may conduct research based on the legitimate interests of the data controller (or third parties), unless these interests are outweighed by the fundamental rights and freedoms of the data subject.

Example: A university clinic carries out a survey on public health trends in breast cancer using health data from medical records of patients in last 20 years, which have been anonymized.

params.text:
Secondary Use of Personal Data for Research Purposes

Legitimate interests may serve as a basis for further processing of personal data within the reasonable expectations of data subjects. If the data was not originally collected based on consent, further processing is permissible only if it serves a compatible purpose (See Article 6 para. 4 GDPR). For example, if health data were collected for the purposes of medical treatment in a hospital, they may as well be used for an epidemiological study.

params.text:
Safeguards and Derogations for Scientific Research

Processing of Special Categories of Data

In principle it is prohibited to process special categories of personal data such as those revealing racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious or philosophical, health data, genetic data, etc. Where in a research projects special categories of personal data are processed, the provision of Article 9 (2) lit. j GDPR will apply in addition to the provisions of Article 6 GDPR. This provides that processing of such categories of data will be lawful, if it is necessary for scientific or historical research purposes or statistical purposes and on the condition that it ‘shall be proportionate to the aim pursued, respect the essence of the right to data protection and provide for suitable and specific measures to safeguard the fundamental rights and the interests of the data subject’.

Another possible derogation from the rules of the GDPR is related to duration requirements. Personal data may be retained for longer periods of time insofar as the personal data will be processed solely for scientific research purposes (Art. 5 (1) lit. e GDPR).

params.text:
Medical Secrecy, Confidentiality, and Exceptions

Medical Secrecy

Medical professional secrecy and confidentiality are established as ethical requirements but are also protected under national law and international instruments such as the Universal Declaration of Bioethics and Human Rights or the WMA International Code of Medical Ethics and others. Respect for patient confidentiality has been affirmed as a professional obligation of physicians since antiquity. Confidentiality is essential for fostering trust, encouraging patients to seek medical care, and ensuring honest communication about their health.

This right provides that information collected by medical professionals from patients during medical care should be treated as confidential, meaning that unauthorized disclosure of information is prohibited. These have a duty to protect patient information from unauthorized persons who have no right to receive such information and thus, they are prohibited from any such disclosure.

Medical secrecy covers all patient-related information, including medical history, diagnostic results, and discussions during consultations. Confidentiality also extends to electronic health records, physical files, and verbal communications. It is noted that, in contrast to data protection rules, medical secrecy extends also to medical information of deceased patients.

Exceptions to Medical Secrecy

Restrictions of the right to confidentiality can be introduced only in specific and limited circumstances. This may be possible if a restriction is established in law, it pursues a legitimate aim, and it is necessary in a democratic society (See Art. 8 para. 2 ECHR). The duty of medical confidentiality is also lifted when the patient consents to disclosures of his/her medical data, e.g. to other doctors or diagnostic centers.

params.text: Patients have the right to access their medical information, and the right to obtain copies of their medical records under the GDPR (Article 15) but also under medical laws, such as the HIPAA in USA or Law 3418/2005 in Greece. This right includes all kinds of health data, including medical history, diagnostic test results, prescriptions, and treatment.

Relatives of a patient can be granted access to his/her medical files only with the patient’s explicit consent. If a patient is unable to give consent, access can be granted to relatives appointed as guardians if they are empowered to make a health decision. After a patient’s death, legal heirs may access medical to settle legal or administrative matters.

params.text:
The Regulation on the European Health Data Space (EHDS) contains provisions regarding access to electronic health data; in general, it institutes a governance framework for the primary and secondary use of electronic health data. Namely, it establishes the EHDS by providing for rules, common standards and practices, infrastructures and a governance framework for the primary and secondary use of electronic health data.

The EHDS provides for the right of natural persons to access their personal electronic health data processed in the context of primary use of electronic health data, immediately, free of charge and in an easily readable, consolidated and accessible form. in addition, they have the right to receive an electronic copy in the electronic health data (EHD) format or at least, their data in the priority categories of personal EHD, i.e., (a) patient summaries, (b) electronic prescriptions, (c) electronic dispensations, (d) medical images and image reports (e) laboratory results and (f)discharge reports.

params.text: Cloud offers many potential benefits for researchers, as it enables efficient, cost effective, and collaborative research. Computing resources can be easily adjusted to match project needs. Hardware and maintenance costs shrink and in, general, researchers can benefit from cost savings but also from the possibility of storing large datasets and using advanced tools (AI, data analysis and visualization software).

When dealing with sensitive data, such as medical or patient information, researchers face stringent legal, ethical, and technical requirements to ensure data protection and privacy. Since, data protection laws and national legislation applies, it must be ensured that the cloud provider complies with the GDPR or the HIPAA in the U.S.

Personal data can be processed for scientific purposes if pseudonymization or anonymization techniques are used. Encryption of data would help to protected stored and prevent interception during transfer. Where localization of data is required, cloud providers with data centers in compliant locations should be chosen.
In case, a data transfer to a third country takes place by the cloud provider, data subjects should be informed and eventually, an informed consent for the use of the cloud should be obtained.
Technical and organizational measures should be taken and, therefore, providers offering specific solutions for sensitive data such as AWS Health or Google Cloud Healthcare API should be preferred.

APPENDIX I: DPIA for Hypothetical Research Project

It follows a detailed outline for developing a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) for a hypothetical research project involving sensitive medical data.
Project Title: The Impact of Genetic Markers on Cardiovascular Disease Risk

• Purpose of the DPIA: Ensure compliance with GDPR by identifying and mitigating risks to the privacy and rights of data subjects involved in the research.
  • Overview of the Research Project:
    • This study aims to analyze the genetic markers of individuals to understand their correlation with cardiovascular disease risk.
    • Data sources include medical records, genetic profiles, and patient-reported lifestyle data.

• Data Categories: 
    • Personal Data: Names, dates of birth, contact details.
    • Special Categories of Data: Genetic data, medical histories, lifestyle information (e.g., smoking habits).
  • Processing Purposes:
    • Scientific research to advance understanding of cardiovascular risks.
    • Publication of anonymized results for academic purposes.
  • Data Collection Methods:
    • Obtained from hospital records and through participant surveys.
  • Retention Period:
    • Personal data will be retained for the duration of the study (5 years) and anonymized data for an indefinite period for future research.

• GDPR Compliance:
    • Processing based on Article 9(2)(j) GDPR (necessary for scientific research purposes).
    • Explicit consent obtained from all participants.

• Data Flow Diagram:
    • Data collected → encrypted transfer to secure servers → processing and analysis by authorized researchers → anonymized datasets for publication.
  • Storage Details:
    • Data stored in an EU-based secure cloud server compliant with GDPR.
    • Physical backups in a locked facility accessible only to the data controller.

Risk: Unauthorized access to data

Likelihood: Medium

Impact: High

Mitigation Measures: Encryption, two-factor authentication.

Risk: Re-identification of anonymized data

Likelihood: Low

Impact: High

Mitigation Measures: Robust anonymization techniques.

Risk: Data breach during transfer

Likelihood: Medium

Impact: High

Mitigation Measures: Use of secure transfer protocols (TLS).

Risk: Improper participant consent

Likelihood: Low

Impact: Medium

Mitigation Measures: Clear and detailed consent forms.

• Technical Measures:
    • Encryption of data both in transit and at rest.
    • Use of pseudonymization for processing.
    • Regular security audits and penetration testing.
  • Organizational Measures:
    • Data access limited to authorized personnel only.
    • Mandatory GDPR training for all researchers.
    • A dedicated Data Protection Officer (DPO) overseeing compliance.

• Transparency: Participants will receive a plain-language information sheet detailing data processing activities.
  • Access and Portability: Participants may request access to their data or request its deletion if permissible.
  • Withdrawal: Participants can withdraw consent at any time without penalty.

• Collaborators: External research organizations will receive anonymized datasets only.
  • Data Sharing Agreements: Formal agreements ensure third parties comply with GDPR.

• Stakeholder Review: This DPIA has been reviewed by the project’s ethics committee, the institutional DPO, and legal advisors.
  • Approval: Signed off by the principal investigator and the DPO.
